analysis.one_liner: Requires Supreme Court justices to follow a binding ethics code, disclose gifts, and step aside from cases involving their benefactors.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee and sat on the Senate calendar with 43 cosponsors, but never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Supreme Court to adopt a binding code of conduct for justices, with a process for investigating ethics complaints. It would have forced justices to disclose gifts, travel, and income at least as rigorously as members of Congress, and to step aside from any case involving a party that gave them money or gifts in the previous six years. It also would have required parties and outside groups to reveal gifts or payments to justices and to disclose who funds their "friend of the court" briefs.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who appears before, or is affected by, the Supreme Court. Litigants would get a real process to demand a justice step aside when a conflict exists, and the public would see justices' gifts and the funding behind the briefs that flood the Court. Currently, justices decide their own recusals and there is no enforceable ethics code for them.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Supreme Court to issue a code of conduct for justices within 180 days and to post it, and any related ethics rules, publicly on its website.

Creates a complaint process: anyone could file an ethics complaint against a justice, and a randomly selected panel of five chief circuit judges would investigate, with subpoena power, and publish its findings.
Requires justices to disclose gifts, income, and reimbursements at least as rigorously as House and Senate disclosure rules apply to members of Congress.

Expands mandatory recusal: a justice must step aside if a party or its affiliate gave the justice, their spouse, or minor child income, gifts, or reimbursements within the previous six years, or lobbied or spent substantial funds to support the justice's confirmation.

Lets parties file disqualification motions that are decided by a reviewing panel rather than by the justice alone; for a Supreme Court justice, the other eight justices would review the motion, and every disqualification must be publicly explained on the court's website.

Requires every party and friend-of-the-court filer to disclose any gift, income, or reimbursement it, its lawyers, or its officers gave any justice, and requires amicus briefs to list their significant funders, with an annual audit.

analysis.who_pays: The justices themselves, who would lose sole control over their own recusal and gift rules; the federal judiciary, which would run the complaint, investigation, and audit systems; and parties, law firms, and interest groups, which would face new disclosure paperwork for gifts to justices and amicus funding. Taxpayers fund the administrative cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Justices, the courts, and interest groups

drawbacks.text: Enforcement is weaker than it looks: the investigation panel only 'presents findings and recommendations' to the Court, and a motion to disqualify a justice would be decided by the other eight justices, so the institution would still largely judge its own members.

The amicus disclosure rules would hit every filer, including small nonprofits and individuals, requiring them to list anyone contributing over $100,000 or 3% of revenue, and the bill lets courts strike briefs that would disqualify a judge — critics argued this burdens participation and treads on judicial independence as a separation-of-powers matter.

The committee's amended version added an unrelated nonbinding section condemning racial attacks on Justice Thomas, which had nothing to do with the ethics machinery and was attached by the committee amendment.
Six-year recusal lookback and gift definitions rely on justices and parties to self-report; the bill depends on honest disclosure, and its studies of compliance would come years apart.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — enforceable ethics rules, gift disclosure, and independent recusal review for the most powerful court in the country — far outweigh the compliance paperwork, and the public would finally see who is paying the justices' way. The honest weakness is structural: the bill still leaves the final word on discipline and disqualification largely inside the Court itself, so a determined institution could blunt it. And the bill never got far enough for any of this to be tested: it died on the Senate calendar.

outcome.mechanism: It was reported out of the Judiciary Committee and placed on the Senate's calendar in September 2023, but no one ever brought it up for a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on February 9, 2023, with 27 original cosponsors; it was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee.
A Judiciary subcommittee held a hearing on the bill on June 14, 2023.

The committee ordered the bill reported favorably on July 20, 2023, and Chairman Durbin reported it on September 5, 2023 with a substitute amendment; it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 199.
The committee amendment added a nonbinding 'sense of Congress' section condemning racially charged attacks on Justice Thomas, alongside the bill's ethics provisions.

The bill's 43 cosponsors were all Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never received a floor vote in the Senate or the House before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The Senate in this period had no ethics legislation for the Supreme Court enacted; the Court itself adopted a voluntary, nonbinding code of conduct in November 2023 without any enforcement mechanism.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The justices, who keep sole control over their own recusal decisions and gift rules, and the wealthy patrons, litigants, and interest groups who benefit from a court that polices itself without outside disclosure or review.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The justices and their gift-giving benefactors

industries.note: The bill would strip justices of sole authority over their own recusals, subject them to an enforceable code of conduct and complaint process, and require gift disclosure at congressional standards. Justices currently set their own ethics rules with no binding enforcement.

industries.industry: Wealthy patrons and litigants who give gifts to justices
industries.note: Anyone who gave a justice income, gifts, or reimbursements within the previous six years, or spent substantial funds backing the justice's confirmation, would trigger that justice's disqualification from their cases. Parties would also have to disclose any gifts their side gave justices. This would directly burden the kind of undisclosed patronage that prompted the bill.

Briefs would have to list significant funders (over $100,000 or 3% of annual revenue), subject to annual audit, and courts could strike briefs whose filers' gifts to a justice would require disqualification. This exposes shadow funding behind Supreme Court advocacy.

industries.industry: Law firms practicing before the Supreme Court
industries.note: Firms and their officers would have to disclose gifts, income, or reimbursements provided to any justice, and lobbying contacts or spending supporting a justice's confirmation. Most of this disclosure burden falls on firms already doing business at the Court.
